audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, initial' (initial stress) rests on McPherson, Daniels & Hendy 2021 sec. 3.1, a 2021 phonology paper by specialist fieldworkers with 100+ hours of primary data; the quotation is verbatim at p. 31 in the copy downloaded now (previously not yet obtained). The statement is explicit (initial stress on content words, with duration/fortition/vowel-reduction correlates, pitch reserved for tone) and the trochaic-foot tone domain in sec. 4 independently supports initial prominence. The only older primary description, Kerr's 1967 MA thesis (Glottolog's 'grammar'; downloaded now, 137 pp), has no stress statement, only footnotes on phonemes and word-level tone; Kerr 1975 is silent. No better or competing source exists per Glottolog (5 refs) and web search. Non-strict/dominant flag is appropriate given the restriction to 'content words' and the coexisting tone system. sources.citation: McPherson, Daniels & Hendy 2021, Lexical and grammatical tone in Wiru, Proc. TAI 2021, sec 3.1 (isca-archive.org PDF, full stress section read)
sources.quote: Wiru content words are characterized by initial stress. On the surface, the stressed syllable is longer, with fully articulated onset consonants, while unstressed syllables are subject to vowel reduction (or elision) and lenition of onset consonants

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura, Don Daniels & Caroline Hendy. 2021. Lexical and grammatical tone in Wiru (Southern Highlands Province, PNG). Proc. 1st International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2021), 31-35. doi:10.21437/TAI.2021-7
sources.quote: 'Wiru content words are characterized by initial stress. On the surface, the stressed syllable is longer, with fully articulated onset consonants, while unstressed syllables are subject to vowel reduction (or elision) and lenition of onset consonants (voicing and/or spirantization).' ... 'Because tone is an independent phonological contrast, stress is not marked with pitch in Wiru.' sources.citation: Kerr, Harland B. 1967. A preliminary statement of Witu grammar: the syntactic role and structure of the verb. MA thesis, University of Hawaii. 137 pp. (ScholarSpace item 10125/36008; = Glottolog refs 12211/12210)
sources.quote: No stress statement. fn. 5: 'Tone is contrastive in Witu, but as in Fasu and possibly other languages in this area of the Highlands it is contrastive at the word rather than the syllable level. A given word carries only one contrastive tone. The over-all tone contour of the word is determined by the nature of the tone, the placement of the tone and the length of the word. There appear to be only two contrastive tones.' fn. 4 notes p, t, k 'tend to be voiceless aspirated word initially, and unaspirated, sometimes with slight friction and voicing, word medially'.
sources.locator: fn. 4 p. 12 (p. 20) segmental phonemes; fn. 5 p. 13 (p. 21) tone

sources.citation: Kerr, Harland B. 1972. Witu-English and English-Witu Dictionary. Unpublished manuscript, 430 pp. (Glottolog ref 680279; SIL, Ukarumpa).
sources.note: Dictionary sections A, K, P, T only, no front matter or key. Headwords carry sporadic acute accents (aabu vs aabú, káa, akolonó, katiká) never explained; one entry (-ta, p.311) says the suffix 'usually takes a high tone' on the first of two moras. No tone inventory or analysis; nothing on stress.

tone.quote: -ta suffix essentially indicates duality It may coordinater two nouns and still be essentially dual in function ... It usually takes a high tone but seems to have two moras of length with the high tone falling on the first mora.
tone.locator: p. 311, letter T, entry -ta; cf. accent-marked headwords aabu vs aabú, p. 2 and káa 'bag' / káa 'track', p. 43

sources.note: Morphosyntax paper with first-hand tone-marked data; per McPherson et al. 2021 sec 5.2 (citing it as [5]) and the Wikipedia summary sourced to it, it reports that the noun-modifying (relative) clause construction imposes a replacive falling {HL} melody on the head noun whatever its lexical tone, i.e. grammatical tone overlaid on a lexical H/L system. Full tone inventory statement not seen.
